passages.t: Judah's clans, and the prayer of Jabez
passages.happening:
More families of Judah are listed, tied to towns such as Bethlehem, Tekoa, Gedor, Eshtemoa, Soco, Keilah and Mareshah (verses 1-8). Then the list stops for one man. ‘Now Jabez was more honorable than his brothers. His mother had named him Jabez’ (verse 9), because she bore him in pain. Jabez calls out to the God of Israel, “If only You would bless me and enlarge my territory! May Your hand be with me and keep me from harm, so that I will be free from pain.” ‘And God granted the request of Jabez’ (verse 10).

The names go on (verses 11-23): Othniel and Caleb's families, craftsmen in the Valley of Craftsmen, linen workers at Beth-ashbea, and ‘the potters who lived at Netaim and Gederah. They lived there in the service of the king’ (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
Nothing else is known of Jabez, not even his father's name. He is remembered only because he prayed. His name sounds like the Hebrew word for pain, otsev, with two letters swapped, and a name like that could feel like a sentence hanging over a life. His prayer asks God to reverse it, in plain terms: land, God's hand, safety. The names on either side of him have no story, and the contrast makes him stand out.

Othniel son of Kenaz was the first of the judges, and Caleb son of Jephunneh the scout who trusted God. The note in verse 22 that these names come from ancient records shows the Chronicler drawing on older sources.

Many families here are known by their work. Trades were often passed down in families and linked with towns. Some scholars connect the royal potters with the many jar handles from Judah stamped with a phrase meaning belonging to the king, from the late eighth century BC, though the link cannot be proved. Mered's wife Bithiah is called Pharaoh's daughter; whether she was a princess or an Egyptian woman of standing is not clear.
passages.later: Paul wrote, ‘Be anxious for nothing, but in everything, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God’ (Philippians 4:6).
passages.hard:
Is the prayer of Jabez a formula for success and prosperity?

In 2000 Bruce Wilkinson's book The Prayer of Jabez became a bestseller, urging Christians to pray these words daily and expect God to expand their influence and their good fortune. Many readers found it an encouragement to pray boldly. Many others, including a large number of pastors and scholars, worried that it turned a short story into a formula and could slide toward prosperity teaching, the idea that God rewards faith with material gain.

The text itself is modest. It reports that one man, remembered as honorable, asked God for land, God's hand and freedom from harm, and that God answered. The Chronicler offers it as an example of a pattern he values: those who call on the God of Israel are heard. Nothing in the passage suggests that repeating Jabez's words guarantees a result, and elsewhere Scripture shows faithful people who prayed and suffered. The best reading lets Jabez teach honest, confident prayer to a God who cares about ordinary needs, and leaves the answer in God's hands.
passages.asks: Jabez asked God to undo the pain spoken over his life. Ask what has been spoken over yours that you have never brought to God. And ask whether your prayers are honest requests or attempts to get a guaranteed result.

passages.t: Simeon, a small tribe looking for pasture
passages.happening:
The descendants of Simeon are listed (verses 24-27), with the note that their clans did not grow as large as Judah's. Their towns are named, Beersheba among them, ‘until the reign of David’ (verses 28-33). A list of leaders follows (verses 34-38).

Some Simeonite clans go to the edge of Gedor in search of pasture for their flocks and find good, quiet land (verses 39-40). ‘These who were noted by name came in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah’ (verse 41), attacked the people living there, and settled in their place. Others go to the hill country of Seir and strike down the last of the Amalekites, ‘And they have lived there to this day’ (verse 43).
passages.hearers:
Simeon's towns closely match those in Joshua, which says Simeon's land lay inside Judah's. Over time Simeon seems to have been absorbed into Judah, which may be why its clans did not grow. Ziklag later passed to David from a Philistine king, which may explain the note about the reign of David.

The expansion is dated to Hezekiah, about 715 to 686 BC. The Meunites were a people of the southern desert, and the Amalekites Israel's old enemies in the south. In a pastoral society pasture was life, and these reports reflect growing clans with limited land. The repeated phrase to this day ties the old events to the situation the first readers knew.

The chapter reports the taking of land by force, as ancient records did, without comment. It gives no one today a warrant to take land from others or to harm any people.
passages.later: Joshua says of the tribe, ‘So the Simeonites received an inheritance within Judah’s portion’ (Joshua 19:9).
passages.asks: The Simeonites went looking for room to live. Ask what pressures push families and peoples to move today. And ask how you treat those who arrive in your town looking for room.
